title: Software
text:
L2-Based Factor Capacity Analysis

Developed by Sheng’en Li · Open-source release in preparation

I developed a factor-capacity evaluation tool that takes a factor signal and generates a PDF report comparing execution feasibility across initial capital levels. The engine uses Level-2 market data to simulate how a strategy’s planned trades translate into simulated holdings under trading constraints.

title: Software
section: From a factor to a capacity report
text:
From a factor to a capacity report

Specify the strategy. Supply the factor signal and the portfolio and trading rules used for the evaluation.
Simulate each capital level. Track orders, cash, and holdings under a volume-participation limit, available-cash and sellable-position constraints, trading suspensions, and price limits.
Inspect the report. Compare the tested capital levels using completion checks, execution diagnostics, and return differences. Partial fills and unfinished orders help identify where execution becomes constrained.

title: Software
text:
What the capacity estimate means
The current evaluation criterion combines a 10% participation limit with 100% same-day completion of planned trades. The reported execution capacity is the largest tested capital level that satisfies this criterion over the evaluation period.
This definition makes the result interpretable: it is tied to a specified factor strategy, market-data period, execution protocol, and set of tested capital levels. A larger account changes order sizes, which can change fills, available cash, and subsequent holdings. Repeating the simulation at each capital level captures these changes in the portfolio’s path.
My focus is the connection between the desired portfolio and the portfolio that can actually be built. The report makes that connection visible alongside the capacity estimate, so a user can inspect which constraints bind as capital increases.

title: Software
text:
Availability
The tool currently runs on company Level-2 data. I am preparing the core engine for open-source release; the public data interface is still being worked out. Code and example-report links will be added when the release is available.

title: When Does a Better Anomaly Score Lead to Better Alarms?
text:
Skip to content
An anomaly detector produces a score. Someone monitoring a system needs a warning while there is still time to respond. Between those two outputs sit several choices: when a score becomes available, whether to act on it immediately, whether to accumulate evidence, and when an existing alarm should count as a new warning. My Signature Work studies this gap by separating the information a detector uses from the decisions made with its scores.

title: When Does a Better Anomaly Score Lead to Better Alarms?
section: The same ranking can yield different warnings
text:
The same ranking can yield different warnings
Consider three events, each lasting four observation blocks. Place one high score at the beginning of each event. A threshold rule can warn during all three. Now move those same three high scores into consecutive blocks of a single event. The positive examples retain exactly the same score distribution, and the negative examples are unchanged. Average precision and AUROC therefore stay fixed, even though the warnings cover fewer events.
In the analytic construction in my thesis, both arrangements have AP 0.750 and AUROC 0.625. The spread arrangement detects three of three events, each after 64 samples. The concentrated arrangement detects one of three, after 128 samples. Consecutive active ticks count as one alarm interval. These are constructed sequences showing what ranking metrics leave unspecified: they retain score–label relationships while discarding the order that determines event coverage and delay.

title: When Does a Better Anomaly Score Lead to Better Alarms?
text:
Hold the scores fixed
This observation also helps distinguish two uses of history. A model can use earlier observations to judge whether the current observation is unusual. An alarm rule can accumulate earlier scores before deciding to warn. To investigate the first, I paired the same raw history and current blocks in different ways. A fixed detector reading only the current block then has identical score distributions in the two classes; any useful distinction must come from their relationship. To investigate the second, I kept the fitted score at every time step fixed and changed the alarm rule.



Two experimental controls: re-pairing shared blocks isolates contextual information; applying different alarm rules to a shared score stream isolates the effect of the decision rule.


For the alarm comparison, a threshold responds to an individual score, while CUSUM accumulates transformed score evidence over time. Both receive scores from the same contextual model trained on normal data. In the primary simulated experiment, each rule uses 50,000 normal calibration ticks, a nominal budget of 100 new alarm onsets per 10,000 ticks, and a 5% alarm-occupancy cap. Each score arrives only after its 64-sample block is complete. A hit requires a new alarm onset during the event; an alarm already active when the event starts receives no credit.

title: When Does a Better Anomaly Score Lead to Better Alarms?
text:
Read recall alongside warning burden
The two simulated transition patterns give the following results with fixed fitted detectors:









Setting
Threshold event recall
CUSUM event recall
Threshold / CUSUM normal onsets




Ring
19.2%
28.8%
98.15 / 94.65


Cluster
7.8%
10.7%
102.85 / 93.45



Recall counts detections within four completed blocks and keeps every event in the denominator. Normal onsets are measured per 10,000 score ticks on independent normal streams. The common calibration target does not make the observed warning costs identical. Reporting those costs beside recall is necessary to understand what each operating point provides.
The recall gains also need a timing explanation. In the ring setting, CUSUM detects 128 events that thresholding misses, while thresholding detects 32 that CUSUM misses, among 1,000 scheduled events. That difference accounts for the 9.6-percentage-point recall gain. On events both rules detect, CUSUM is usually equally fast or slower. Its advantage comes from covering additional events. A utility measure that includes misses and rewards earlier warnings improves clearly for ring; the corresponding cluster interval includes zero.

title: When Does a Better Anomaly Score Lead to Better Alarms?
text:
What changes in real series
Evaluation on 119 real series from five sources makes the operating-point issue more visible. Accumulation provides no consistent detection gain. In the eight-sample-block comparison, CUSUM reduces both mean event recall and warnings during normal-labeled periods on four sources. Those warning counts describe the normal-labeled portions of mixed streams, where alarm state can carry over from an event. They answer a different question from the independent normal-stream rates in the simulation.
For me, a convincing claim about better alarms needs a paired explanation: which events were gained or lost, when the shared detections occurred, and what warning burden accompanied the change. A useful next comparison would examine event coverage and timing across overlapping ranges of measured warning burden. That would help distinguish benefits from accumulated evidence from changes caused by operating at a different alarm cost. A better score creates an opportunity; the deadline and decision rule determine how much of that opportunity reaches the person monitoring the system.

title: Research
section: Counterfactual Learning for Adaptive Decision Systems
text:
Counterfactual Learning for Adaptive Decision Systems



COPF · Protocol flowchart



Duke Kunshan University / Duke University · Jan. 2025 – Present
Advised by Prof. Dongmian Zou and Prof. Fan Wei

Online recommenders change the graph and feedback they later learn from, so fairness measured on logged outcomes can drift after deployment. I developed COPF, a decision-layer framework that combines explicit exploration and propensity logging with graph-aware doubly robust estimation. An online multicalibration auditor and primal–dual controller then monitor and adjust group-level exposure disparities.
Evaluations on two Temporal Graph Benchmark streams and a controlled synthetic stream show reduced worst-case disparity spikes with modest effects on ranking utility. I am extending this work in COMET to study counterfactual moments under weak overlap and dependent feedback.

Paper · ICML 2026 · Code · First author

title: Research
text:
Taylor-Model Reachability for Neural-Network-Controlled Systems



NN control and flowpipes Illustration: Xiangru Zhong



University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign · May 2026 – Present
Research collaboration with Prof. Huan Zhang’s group

I am developing a PyTorch Taylor-model engine for safety verification of neural-network-controlled systems. The engine propagates polynomial approximations together with validated remainder bounds through nonlinear ODEs, combining interval arithmetic and Picard iteration. My work includes step-level comparisons against Flow* to diagnose polynomial truncation, remainder growth, enclosure tightness, and CPU/GPU consistency.
The broader project connects GPU-batched flowpipes to CROWN-type neural-network verifiers through certified polynomial couplings. These interfaces preserve dependencies that interval-only bounds discard, helping assess how numerical precision and controller bounds affect the reachable sets used to certify safety.

title: Research
section: Audit–Refine Partial-Physics Models for ECG-Based Electrolyte Inference
text:
Audit–Refine Partial-Physics Models for ECG-Based Electrolyte Inference



Audit–Refine · Framework overview



Duke Kunshan University · Mar. 2026 – Aug. 2026
Advised by Prof. Shixin Xu and Prof. Dongmian Zou

I co-developed an Audit–Refine framework for testing whether a partial-physics model’s mechanistic scaffold is supported by data. In ECG-based electrolyte inference, a projective Plausibility Index measures waveform alignment, while tangent and Fisher-information diagnostics assess whether electrolyte concentrations can be recovered locally. The framework combines matched null models, held-out inverse error, residual structure, and robustness checks to decide which refinements to accept.
I built and validated analyte-specific MIMIC-IV-ECG pipelines and evaluated reduced-rank potassium refinements. Four of seven electrolyte–scaffold hypotheses passed the audit; the accepted potassium spline reduced held-out MAE from 0.417 to 0.396 mEq/L, a 5.0% relative improvement.

Submitted to Artificial Intelligence in Medicine · Co-first author

title: Research
section: Contextual Information and Alarm Utility in Time-Series Anomaly Detection
text:
Contextual Information and Alarm Utility in Time-Series Anomaly Detection



Signature Work · Experimental design



Duke Kunshan University · 2025 – 2026
Signature Work · Advised by Prof. Dongmian Zou

My Signature Work separates three questions in anomaly detection: what temporal context adds, how much evidence a model captures, and when its scores produce useful warnings. I designed matched-block experiments that preserve observed data while changing history–current pairings, proving chance-level ranking for fixed current-only detectors. A covariance-based Markov model trained on normal data measures the value of contextual relationships.
I compare thresholding and accumulation on identical scores, tracking event recall, detection delay, and warning burden. CUSUM increased four-block recall by 9.6 and 2.9 percentage points in two simulated settings. Evaluation across 119 real series from five sources found no consistent detection gain from accumulation, highlighting the need to evaluate recall alongside the frequency of warnings during normal periods.

Research note: from anomaly scores to useful alarms

title: Research
text:
Fair Graph Anomaly Detection



DECAF-GAD · Model architecture



Duke Kunshan University · Jul. 2024 – May 2025
Summer Research Scholar · Advised by Prof. Dongmian Zou

Graph autoencoders can mistake differences between demographic groups for anomalies. I co-developed DECAF-GAD, a fairness-aware framework that uses a structural causal model to separate sensitive information from the representations used for detection. A shared encoder processes original and counterfactual graphs, while disentanglement, adversarial learning, and counterfactual consistency losses guide reconstruction.
The framework can be added to existing autoencoder-based detectors. Through experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs and component ablations, we evaluated the fairness–utility trade-off and found improved fairness metrics while maintaining competitive anomaly detection performance.

Paper · ECAI 2025 · Code · Co-first author

title: When Does a Factor Become Too Large to Trade?
text:
Skip to content
A factor signal, together with portfolio-construction rules, defines the positions a strategy aims to hold. Increasing the capital allocated to it also increases the trading needed to reach those positions. My question is how far that allocation can grow while the trading plan remains executable under a stated set of rules. Answering it requires following the orders through time: the intended portfolio alone does not tell me which positions the strategy can actually acquire or unwind.
I developed a tool that takes a factor as input, runs execution backtests at multiple initial-capital levels using Level 2 market data, and produces a PDF capacity report. The current evaluation uses a 10% participation-rate limit and requires 100% of each day’s planned trading to finish that day. These settings give the experiment an explicit pass condition. A run that leaves an order unfinished fails that completion requirement, even if most of its planned trading succeeds.

title: When Does a Factor Become Too Large to Trade?
text:
Follow the portfolio through execution
The execution simulation tracks fills and maintains the state needed to decide whether orders can fill. That state includes cash and sellable shares, alongside the restrictions associated with suspensions and daily price limits. Partial fills change the portfolio immediately; unfinished orders remain unfinished. This matters because a target weight is only a request. A backtest must account for the holdings and available resources that emerge as the request is executed.
Consider two runs with identical factor inputs but different starting capital. Both receive the same instruction to sell one position and buy another. The larger run requests more shares and needs more execution opportunities within the participation limit. If its sale fills only partially, it retains more of the old position and receives less cash than the plan anticipated. A subsequent purchase must use the cash actually available. The two runs can therefore follow different holding paths even though their factor rankings and target weights agree. Scaling capital changes the sequence of attainable portfolios.

title: When Does a Factor Become Too Large to Trade?
section: Execution opportunities have a time window
text:
Execution opportunities have a time window
Timing also explains why a full day’s trading volume is insufficient to establish capacity. Consider an order submitted late in the session for a stock that traded heavily earlier that morning. The earlier trades contribute to daily volume, but they provide no execution opportunity for an instruction that did not yet exist. The relevant sequence begins after that instruction and ends at its deadline. Applying the participation rule to the opportunities within that sequence can leave the order incomplete despite a large daily total. Available cash, sellable shares, and trading restrictions further determine which of those opportunities the simulated strategy can use.

title: When Does a Factor Become Too Large to Trade?
text:
Define the capacity criterion
For this tool, capacity is the largest tested capital level that passes the execution criteria over the evaluated data period. The word “tested” is essential. A capital grid produces verdicts for its individual levels; it does not establish an exact optimum between them. The reported value belongs to that grid, that period, and those execution rules. Changing the trading deadline or participation limit changes the question being evaluated. I therefore report the estimate together with the evaluation period and execution settings.
I separate this completion test from the judgment that trading costs are acceptable. An order may finish within the participation limit while the economics of executing it remain unattractive. Conversely, an attractive intended portfolio does not compensate for trades that cannot finish. The current completion criterion answers a feasibility question. Assessing whether the executed strategy is worth allocating capital to requires a further cost judgment.
The question I want the report to make answerable is where feasibility is lost as capital increases. A volume constraint, an incomplete sale, and a purchase blocked by available cash can all leave a plan unfinished, but they point to different changes in the strategy. Tracing those constraints connects a capacity estimate to an explanation of the portfolio that was actually attainable.
The core engine is being prepared for open-source release. The project page describes the current workflow and availability.

title: Why I Built Reader First
text:
Skip to content
I built Reader First because I want explanations that let me keep reading. A technical answer can contain the right facts and still require work to connect them: a condition arrives after the claim it limits, several nouns conceal an action, or “this” could refer to three different things. My aim was to make that work visible to the writer. If the writer already knows how the pieces fit together, some of those relationships can be stated directly.
A study by Clark, Martin, and Mahowald gave me a useful starting point. They examine English features associated with processing difficulty, including long syntactic dependencies and stacked nouns. Across chat and coding in particular, many models used longer dependencies and more stacked nouns than their round-trip paraphrases, although the pattern varied by model, feature, and setting. A separate experiment shows that a length penalty can shift a small model toward shorter grammatical variants. The study measures linguistic features and model preferences; it does not directly test human comprehension of the generated passages.

title: Why I Built Reader First
section: Spend words where they help the reader
text:
Spend words where they help the reader
The design question I took from this was how to spend words where they help someone follow a thought. A reader meets a sentence in sequence. An explanation should introduce the object under discussion, make its action clear, and place the relevant conditions where they can guide interpretation. I made the skill’s objective explicit: reduce the extra inference and rereading needed to recover the intended meaning. That gives each proposed edit a purpose beyond changing the sound of the prose.
The following is an illustrative example from the skill, translated into English. It was written to explain an editing decision; it is neither a quotation from the paper nor a report of an actual test.

Dense version: I added three concurrent-write cache-invalidation regression tests, all passing locally; production reliability under high load remains unverified.


Expanded version: I added three regression tests to check whether the cache is invalidated as expected during concurrent writes. All three tests passed locally. Reliability under high production load has not been verified.

The expanded version gives “tests” an explicit purpose and makes concurrent writing a condition of the check. Repeating “three tests” keeps the local result attached to the work just described. The final sentence identifies the remaining question. The technical content survives: there are three tests, they concern invalidation during concurrent writes, they passed locally, and production reliability remains unverified. Invalidation also keeps its technical meaning: making a cached value unusable when appropriate. Replacing it with “cache failure” would change the claim.
This example also shows why I constrain expansion to relationships the source already supplies. A compressed phrase about timeouts, retries, and fallback may leave their order unspecified. Writing a smooth story in which retries fail and a backup service takes over would introduce behavior that has not been established. I therefore put a meaning check before the readability check. The editor must preserve conditions, quantities, negation, evidence, and uncertainty while deciding how to arrange them.

title: Why I Built Reader First
text:
Adapt the principle to Chinese
Chinese needed its own treatment. The original example contains the phrase “三个并发写入场景下的缓存失效回归测试.” Before reaching “tests,” the reader has already encountered the number, operating condition, cache operation, and test category. My revision names the tests first, then explains what they check. That is a decision about when information becomes useful. I also allow a concrete noun to recur when “这,” “其,” or “上述” could point to several objects. Keeping a concept’s name stable can be worth the repetition.
These Chinese rules are my practical extension of the motivation. English advice about an optional that cannot simply become a rule for adding or removing “的.” I want the editor to locate the actual difficulty: a long modifier, an unclear reference, or an unstated condition. Sometimes a short clause resolves it. Sometimes the existing sentence is already clear. The skill consequently has no fixed sentence-length limit or target number of technical terms.
I wanted that flexibility to extend to the reader. Someone familiar with systems programming can usually work with “garbage collector” without a replacement definition. A reader learning the mechanism may need a brief explanation of its role. The same principle governs detail: keep what the reader needs to understand the claim, and remove commentary that adds no useful relationship. Splitting every sentence or turning every paragraph into bullets would create a different obstacle by making the reader reconnect fragments.

title: Why I Built Reader First
text:
Keep the claim intact
For technical work, I gave particular attention to completion states. A proposed change, an edited file, a test that passed locally, and a deployed fix are different facts. An explanation becomes less useful if polishing makes those states interchangeable. Reader First asks for the supported result first, with its scope close by, followed by the reason or evidence needed to assess it. This is where readability and factual precision need to work together.

title: Why I Built Reader First
text:
What I would evaluate next
I regard the skill as a set of editing decisions to examine in use. A meaningful evaluation would ask independent readers the same content questions and record misunderstandings and places where they needed to reread. Those observations could show which expansions help and which merely add length. For now, the design is available to inspect: preserve the claim, find the relationship that costs effort to reconstruct, and make that relationship explicit.
